title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Using the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) under shared_initial_candidate semantics, we ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All archived scoring artifacts report safe outcomes for every paired episode: baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples; reported seed archived); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced identical shared LLM candidates that passed deterministic validation in every task, no validator‑triggered repairs occurred and the primary paired contrast was uninformative. We present the preregistered design, per‑run execution accounting, artifact‑grounded analysis, a mechanistic explanation for the null paired outcome, and concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Automating translation of high‑level operator intent into device configurations is a central NetOps objective. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows increasingly propose multi‑step configuration plans, but token‑level fidelity metrics do not capture ordering, dependency constraints, and operational invariants required for safe application in live networks. Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluation—where generated configurations are executed against device images or simulators and deterministically scored—exposes semantic failure modes (ordering errors, transient violations, protected‑resource touches) that text‑only tests miss.

A common architectural remedy is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM generates a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants, and an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate when violations are detected. Prior work shows GVR‑style patterns can address many syntactic and some semantic faults, but open questions remain about the empirical benefit of integrating deterministic verifiers under distribution shift and adversarial prompts, and about experimental designs that reliably produce informative, paired contrasts between guarded and unguarded pipelines.

This paper reports a fully preregistered paired experiment that measured one precisely defined estimand (the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate: guarded minus baseline) executed under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused across arms). Our contributions are: (1) an artifact‑grounded execution and analysis of the preregistered paired GVR test (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01); (2) a transparent mapping from the preregistered estimand to archived analysis outputs and exact numeric results; and (3) a failure analysis that explains the observed null paired outcome and provides concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.
sections.related_work:
Recent work advocates executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks to evaluate LLM agents in closed‑loop NetOps workflows rather than relying on text similarity metrics [1]. Several system and program‑repair papers describe generate–validate and generate–validate–repair patterns and report substantial repair coverage for many benchmarked error classes, while noting limitations for semantics‑heavy faults [2], [4]. Surveys and position pieces synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising directions to increase operational trustworthiness of NetOps agents [3], [5]. Configuration analysis tools and incremental verification frameworks (for example, Batfish) provide engineering precedent and concrete techniques for deterministic checking and reachability analysis [6].

Our study differs by combining (a) a preregistered paired estimand, (b) preregistered shared_initial_candidate generation semantics, (c) emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring, and (d) full archival of per‑call traces, verifier traces, and analysis artifacts so that the measured estimand is fully traceable to archived outputs. The related literature motivates the GVR pattern and the need to examine its empirical effects under distribution shift and adversarial probes [1]–[6].
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, i.e., the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 denotes a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied and safe_apply = 0 denotes no such violation. Analysis used a paired, binary test executor with bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples) and an exact McNemar test for discordant pairs.

Design and generation semantics: The design is paired with shared_initial_candidate semantics: the adapter produces exactly one initial LLM generation per task and both arms (baseline and guarded) reuse that same generation; the guarded arm may request up to one deterministic‑validator‑triggered repair. The preregistration specified N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks blocked into topology/vendor clusters with the following composition: in‑distribution 60% (144 tasks), distribution‑shift 20% (48 tasks), adversarial‑prompt 20% (48 tasks). Tasks were generated deterministically by the registered task generator and include initial network state, per‑task constraints, and required command sequences.

Model, adapter, and validator: Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini via the hosted adapter family (hosted_netops_gvr_v1). The guarded pipeline invoked deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the deterministic verifier; the adapter permitted up to one repair invocation per task when the verifier flagged a violation. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics a paired contrast can only arise if the single shared candidate fails the verifier or if the guarded arm applies a repair that changes the final configuration relative to the baseline.

Scoring, exclusions, and missingness: The deterministic validator produces a binary final outcome (safe vs unsafe) determined by emulation execution and a set of semantic invariant checks captured in per‑task validator traces. The preregistration declared explicit exclusion rules: pairs flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator unsafe outcome) would be excluded from primary analysis and handled in sensitivity analyses; infra failures after the allowed retry policy would be marked and excluded per the preregistered plan. The preregistered retry policy allowed up to two automatic infra reruns; the primary analysis uses complete pairs after exclusions.

Statistical plan and mapping: The primary analysis executor reports the paired contingency counts (n11, n10, n01, n00), risk difference, 95% bootstrap CI, and exact McNemar p‑value. All analysis parameters (bootstrap resamples, seed) and CSV summaries were archived so that reported numeric results are traceable to the archived artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed per the preregistered plan. Planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480; complete pairs = 240. The provider audit confirms exactly one shared initial generation per task (hosted model calls = 240) consistent with the shared_initial_candidate contract. No infra failures, no unscorable episodes, and no preregistered exclusions occurred.

Primary binary outcomes and contingency: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Condition summaries show baseline successes = 240, baseline failures = 0; guarded successes = 240, guarded failures = 0. The paired contingency is n11 = 240, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Therefore the paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. The 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples) is [0.00, 0.00], and the exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied (repair attempts observed = 0). Representative validator traces show recorded difficulty labels ("very_hard"/"extreme"), required command counts, and final_state snapshots; in every case the shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation and thus both arms produced identical final configurations.

Planned sensitivity channels: The preregistration included sensitivity analyses for 'possible false‑safe' flags and infra failures treated as unsafe in worst‑case analyses; none of these flags were triggered and the contamination summary is empty. Subgroup slices by in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, and adversarial tasks are degenerate (all zeros) given the universal safe outcome across tasks.
sections.discussion:
Mechanistic cause of the null paired contrast: Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics, the generator produced a single shared candidate per task; the guarded arm could only differ from baseline if that shared candidate failed validation or if a validator‑triggered repair modified the candidate. In this run every shared candidate passed deterministic validation, and no repairs were invoked; consequently no discordant pairs could arise and the paired contrast is degenerate. This mechanistic, artifact‑grounded explanation is directly supported by the provider audit, validator traces, and the archived contingency table.

Design tradeoffs and operational implications: Shared_initial_candidate semantics reduces model‑call budget and ensures direct pairing of an LLM sample, but it also constrains causal contrastability: verifier benefit is only observable when the shared candidate contains a violation. To measure verifier effectiveness as a causal intervention, future designs should consider one or more of the following (artifact‑grounded) changes: (A) allow independent initial generations per arm so generator variability can produce discordant outcomes; (B) increase adversary strength or diversify adversarial protocols to create more generator failures for the verifier to catch; (C) expand the repair budget (allow multiple repair iterations) and instrument repair traces to study repair dynamics.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is affected by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate choice; archive artifacts document contract adherence. Construct validity depends on the validator's semantic coverage; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 encodes a finite rule set and may not cover all semantic fault classes. External validity is limited because the task bank is a synthetic, NetConfArena‑style emulation corpus; extrapolation to diverse production vendor ecosystems and operator workflows requires further study. Conclusion validity: the observed baseline unsafe rate of zero prevents detection of a positive verifier benefit in this particular design.

Recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations (artifact‑grounded): (1) If the objective is a paired causal estimate of verifier value, avoid shared_initial_candidate semantics or permit independent generation in at least one arm. (2) Increase the repair iteration budget and instrument repair prompts and edits to analyze repair search behavior. (3) Employ stronger, adaptive adversary protocols to increase the rate of generator failures for the verifier to catch. (4) Enhance verifier semantic coverage and add cross‑checks between verifier PASS and emulator outcomes to detect potential false‑safe cases.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe), yielding paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics constrained the experiment mechanistically: because a single shared initial candidate per task was used and all shared candidates passed deterministic validation, no validator‑triggered repairs were exercised and the primary paired contrast was uninformative. The archived execution and analysis artifacts support these conclusions and provide concrete guidance for future experiments that seek informative paired contrasts by varying generation semantics, adversary strength, or repair budgets.

disclosure_statement: Execution used the declared hosted model "gpt-5-mini" via the registered adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the guarded pipeline employed deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock. Human role and autonomy boundary: before the lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; all literature search, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock. The registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); under that contract the paired contrast could only differ if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. The initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Archived execution and analysis artifacts (execution manifest, per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis CSVs) are available in the experiment artifact bundle referenced by the preregistration; no manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across other models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected and potential validator PASS vs emulator mismatches require additional cross‑checks in future work.
